## Learning Objectives

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Explain the difference between descriptive analytics and analytical modeling and identify accounting situations where each is appropriate.
2. Apply correlation and regression analysis using the Data Analysis ToolPak to examine relationships between accounting variables and evaluate the reliability of the results.
3. Build a trend analysis from historical accounting data and use it to produce a short-term forecast with documented assumptions.
4. Construct a cost-volume-profit model in Excel that links revenue, variable costs, fixed costs, and profit into an integrated framework.
5. Use Scenario Manager, data tables, and Goal Seek to perform what-if analysis and identify the conditions under which accounting outcomes change.
6. Apply Solver to determine an optimal product mix subject to capacity and cost constraints, and perform sensitivity analysis on key assumptions.

---

## Opening Scenario

You are a cost analyst at Charles River, a Boston-area company that designs and sells home furnishings and manufactures selected furniture lines in-house. The vice president of operations has asked you to prepare a financial analysis for the upcoming planning meeting. Three questions are on the agenda. First, the sales team wants a forecast of next quarter's revenue based on recent trends, along with a clear statement of the assumptions behind the projection. Second, the product management team wants to understand how changes in material costs and selling prices would affect the profitability of the furniture product line. Third, the production planning team wants to know the best combination of manufactured furniture items to produce next quarter given limited work center hours and warehouse space. Each question requires you to move beyond describing what has already happened and into the territory of analysis and modeling. You need to build regression models, construct what-if scenarios, and solve optimization problems, all within Excel. This chapter teaches you the techniques that make that work possible.

---

## From Description to Analysis

Chapter 6 focused on descriptive analytics, the process of summarizing historical data into totals, averages, distributions, and comparisons. Descriptive analytics answers the question "what happened?" and forms the foundation of most accounting work. This chapter takes the next step. The techniques here answer questions about relationships ("does revenue increase when we spend more on marketing?"), about the future ("what will next quarter's revenue likely be?"), and about decisions ("what product mix maximizes our profit given our constraints?"). These are the questions that move accounting from reporting into analysis and from analysis into decision support.

The distinction between description and modeling matters because the two activities involve different levels of judgment and different types of risk. A PivotTable that summarizes last quarter's revenue by item group is a factual statement about the past. A regression model that projects next quarter's revenue is an estimate about the future that depends on assumptions about the stability of historical patterns. A cost-volume-profit model that evaluates three pricing strategies is a structured form of reasoning that depends on assumptions about cost behavior, demand elasticity, and market conditions. When accountants produce models rather than summaries, they take on a responsibility to document their assumptions, test their sensitivity to changes, and communicate the limits of their conclusions. This chapter teaches both the technical tools and the professional practices that support responsible modeling.

The academic literature supports the growing importance of analytical modeling in accounting practice. Appelbaum, Kogan, Vasarhelyi, and Yan (2017) identified predictive analytics as an area where accounting professionals increasingly need competence, particularly in audit settings where analytical procedures require the auditor to develop independent expectations for account balances. The Institute of Management Accountants (IMA, 2019) included forecasting, cost modeling, and scenario analysis among the core competencies for management accountants, noting that these skills support planning, budgeting, and strategic decision-making. The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA, 2017) recognized the role of regression and trend analysis in audit data analytics, recommending that auditors use these techniques to set expectations for substantive analytical procedures.

The techniques in this chapter draw on two Charles River table groups. The Order-to-Cash group provides the historical sales data for correlation, regression, and trend analysis. Its SalesInvoice and SalesInvoiceLine tables record the company's billed revenue over time, which makes them well suited for introducing forecasting concepts. The Manufacturing group, together with the Item master in the Master Data group, provides the cost, pricing, and production data for cost-volume-profit modeling and optimization. The Item table includes both StandardCost and ListPrice columns, the ProductionCompletion and ProductionCompletionLine tables record completed production quantities and their standard cost, and the WorkOrderClose table records the manufacturing variance resolved at close. These tables provide the detail needed to build realistic cost and production models for the furniture lines that Charles River manufactures in-house.

## Correlation Analysis in Accounting

Before building a model that uses one variable to predict another, it is good practice to examine whether the two variables are related at all. Correlation analysis measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two numeric variables. The result is a single number called the correlation coefficient, typically denoted as r, that ranges from negative one to positive one. A value near positive one indicates a strong positive relationship, meaning that when one variable increases, the other tends to increase as well. A value near negative one indicates a strong negative relationship, meaning that when one variable increases, the other tends to decrease. A value near zero indicates little or no linear relationship.

In accounting, correlation analysis has several practical applications. A financial analyst might examine the correlation between monthly revenue and the number of sales invoices to determine whether revenue growth is driven by more transactions or by larger transactions. A cost accountant might examine the correlation between production volume and total manufacturing cost to assess whether cost behaves as a variable cost. An auditor performing analytical procedures might examine the correlation between a client's monthly revenue and an independent economic indicator to determine whether external data can serve as a basis for setting expectations.

Excel provides the CORREL function for calculating the correlation coefficient between two ranges of values. The syntax is =CORREL(array1, array2), where array1 and array2 are the two columns of data you want to compare. The two arrays must have the same number of values. For example, if you have monthly revenue in one column and monthly invoice counts in another, =CORREL(B2:B13, C2:C13) returns the correlation coefficient between the two variables over the twelve-month period.

Interpreting the correlation coefficient requires judgment. There are no universal cutoffs that define a "strong" or "weak" correlation, and the interpretation depends on the context. In accounting, correlations above 0.70 (or below negative 0.70) are generally considered strong enough to suggest a meaningful relationship worth investigating further. Correlations between 0.40 and 0.70 suggest a moderate relationship, and correlations below 0.40 suggest a weak or negligible relationship. These are guidelines, not rules, and the substantive question always matters more than the number itself.

> **[WATCH OUT]**
> Correlation measures the strength of a linear relationship only. Two variables can have a strong nonlinear relationship (for example, a U-shaped curve) and still produce a correlation coefficient near zero. More importantly, correlation does not imply causation. A high correlation between advertising spending and revenue does not prove that advertising causes revenue to increase. There may be a third variable, such as seasonal demand, that drives both. In accounting work, always consider alternative explanations before drawing conclusions from a correlation.

The Data Analysis ToolPak also provides a Correlation tool that calculates the correlation matrix for multiple variables at once. To use it, go to the Data tab, click Data Analysis, and select Correlation. In the dialog box, specify the input range containing all the variables you want to compare, indicate whether the first row contains labels, and specify an output location. Excel will produce a table showing the correlation between every pair of variables. This is useful when you want to explore relationships among several variables before deciding which ones to include in a regression model.

The matrix is symmetric, with 1.000 along the diagonal. Strong correlations are highlighted.]*

> **[IN PRACTICE]**
> Auditors use correlation analysis as part of the expectation-setting process in analytical procedures. AU-C Section 520 (AICPA, 2020) requires auditors to develop an expectation for the balance or ratio being tested. When the auditor can identify an independent variable that is highly correlated with the account balance, that variable can serve as a predictor in a regression-based analytical procedure, which provides stronger audit evidence than a simple trend comparison.

## Regression Analysis with the Data Analysis ToolPak

Correlation tells you that two variables are related, but it does not tell you the nature of that relationship in a form you can use to make predictions. Regression analysis takes the next step. It produces a mathematical equation that describes how changes in one variable (the independent variable, or predictor) are associated with changes in another variable (the dependent variable, or outcome). The simplest form is simple linear regression, which fits a straight line through the data points and produces an equation in the form y = a + bx, where y is the predicted value of the dependent variable, a is the intercept (the value of y when x equals zero), b is the slope (the amount y changes for each one-unit increase in x), and x is the value of the independent variable.

In accounting, regression analysis supports several important tasks. Financial analysts use it to forecast revenue based on historical trends or economic indicators. Cost accountants use it to estimate the fixed and variable components of a mixed cost, a technique known as the high-low method's statistical alternative. Auditors use it as the basis for substantive analytical procedures, where the regression model provides the "expected" value against which the recorded balance is compared. In each case, the regression model translates a historical pattern into a forward-looking estimate.

### Enabling the Data Analysis ToolPak

The regression tools are part of the Data Analysis ToolPak, an Excel add-in that must be enabled before first use. To enable it, go to the File tab, click Options, select Add-ins from the left panel, confirm that "Excel Add-ins" is selected in the Manage dropdown at the bottom, and click Go. In the Add-Ins dialog, check the box next to "Analysis ToolPak" and click OK. After enabling the ToolPak, a "Data Analysis" button appears in the Analysis group on the Data tab. You only need to enable the ToolPak once; it remains active for all future workbooks.

*[Figure 7.3: Screenshot of the Excel Add-Ins dialog box with the Analysis ToolPak checkbox selected. An annotation points to the checkbox and notes that this step needs to be done only once.]*

### Running a Simple Linear Regression

To run a regression, click Data Analysis on the Data tab and select Regression from the list. The Regression dialog box asks for several inputs. The Input Y Range is the column containing the dependent variable (the variable you want to predict). The Input X Range is the column containing the independent variable (the predictor). If your ranges include labels in the first row, check the "Labels" checkbox. The Output Range specifies where Excel should place the results. You can also check boxes for residual plots and normal probability plots, which are useful for evaluating the quality of the model.

After you click OK, Excel produces a regression output with three sections. The first section, Regression Statistics, contains the Multiple R (the correlation coefficient), R Square (the proportion of variation in the dependent variable explained by the model), Adjusted R Square (which accounts for the number of predictors), Standard Error (the average distance between the predicted and actual values), and the number of observations. The second section is the ANOVA table, which tests whether the overall regression model is statistically significant. The third section, Coefficients, shows the intercept and slope along with their standard errors, t-statistics, and p-values. The p-value for the slope coefficient is the most important number in this section for practical purposes. A p-value below 0.05 indicates that the relationship between the independent and dependent variables is statistically significant at the 95% confidence level.

*[Figure 7.4: Annotated regression output from the Data Analysis ToolPak. Three sections are labeled: Regression Statistics (with R Square highlighted), ANOVA table (with the Significance F value highlighted), and Coefficients (with the Intercept, Slope, and p-values highlighted). Annotations explain what each value means in plain language.]*

### Interpreting Regression Results

The R Square value tells you how well the model fits the data. An R Square of 0.85, for example, means that 85% of the variation in the dependent variable is explained by the independent variable, and 15% is unexplained. In accounting applications, the acceptable R Square depends on the context. For cost estimation, where the relationship between volume and cost is expected to be strong, an R Square above 0.80 is typically expected. For revenue forecasting, where many factors influence revenue beyond the single predictor in the model, an R Square of 0.60 to 0.75 may be acceptable. The key is to evaluate the R Square relative to the decision being supported and to acknowledge unexplained variation as a source of uncertainty in the model's predictions.

The slope coefficient tells you the direction and magnitude of the relationship. If you are regressing monthly revenue on the number of sales invoices, a slope of 525 means that each additional invoice is associated with $525 in additional revenue. The intercept represents the predicted value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is zero. In many accounting applications, the intercept has a meaningful interpretation. In cost estimation, the intercept represents the estimated fixed cost component, the portion of total cost that does not vary with the activity level.

> **[CONNECTING THE DOTS]**
> In Chapter 11, you will learn SQL window functions that calculate period-over-period changes directly in a query against the Charles River database. The SQL approach is complementary to the regression approach taught here. SQL window functions efficiently compute the raw changes (this quarter versus last quarter) by reading the SalesInvoice and SalesInvoiceLine tables, while regression analysis models the trend across multiple periods and produces a prediction equation. Auditors often use both techniques: SQL to extract the historical data and calculate period changes, and Excel regression to model the trend and set the expectation for the analytical procedure.

## Trend Analysis and Forecasting

Regression against a time variable is one form of trend analysis, but Excel provides additional tools that make trend work more accessible. The TREND function returns predicted values based on a linear regression without requiring you to run the Data Analysis ToolPak. The FORECAST.LINEAR function provides a point forecast for a single new x-value. And Excel's trendline feature adds a fitted line directly to a chart, allowing you to visualize the trend and extend it into the future.

### The TREND and FORECAST.LINEAR Functions

The TREND function takes three or four arguments: known_y's (the historical dependent variable values), known_x's (the historical independent variable values), new_x's (the x-values for which you want predictions), and an optional constant argument. The function returns an array of predicted y-values for the new x-values. For the Charles River monthly revenue example, =TREND(C4:C27, B4:B27, B28:B30) would return the predicted revenue for months 25, 26, and 27 in a single formula. Because TREND returns an array, you enter it as a dynamic array formula in a cell, and the results spill into adjacent cells.

The FORECAST.LINEAR function is simpler and returns a single predicted value. The syntax is =FORECAST.LINEAR(x, known_y's, known_x's). To predict revenue for month 25, you would enter =FORECAST.LINEAR(25, C4:C27, B4:B27). This function produces the same result as substituting x = 25 into the regression equation, but without requiring you to know the equation's coefficients. FORECAST.LINEAR is convenient for quick predictions, but it does not provide the diagnostic information (R Square, p-values, residuals) that the Data Analysis ToolPak produces. For professional analytical work, running the full regression and documenting the diagnostics is the better practice.

### Trendlines on Charts

Excel's trendline feature adds a fitted line to an existing chart. Right-click any data point on the scatter chart you created in Tutorial 7.1, select "Add Trendline," and choose "Linear" from the options. The trendline dialog also allows you to display the equation on the chart (the same y = a + bx equation from the regression) and the R-squared value. You can also set the "Forward" option to extend the trendline beyond the data, which visually projects the forecast into future periods.

Trendlines are useful for presentations because they allow the audience to see both the historical data and the projected trend in a single chart. However, the visual simplicity of a trendline can be misleading. The line suggests a precision that the model may not warrant, especially when the data has high variability around the trend. When using trendlines in professional reports, always accompany the chart with a written discussion of the model's R Square, the magnitude of the residuals, and the assumptions underlying the projection.

*[Figure 7.7: The Charles River monthly revenue scatter chart with a linear trendline added. The equation and R-squared value are displayed on the chart. The trendline is extended three periods forward, with the forecast region shaded in light gray to distinguish it from the historical data.]*

> **[IN PRACTICE]**
> Financial analysts preparing going-concern assessments use trend analysis to project revenue and cash flows for the forecast period. AU-C Section 570 (AICPA, 2020) requires auditors evaluating going concern to consider management's plans, which often include revenue projections. An auditor who independently builds a trend model from the client's historical data and compares it to management's projection is performing a higher-quality analytical procedure than one who simply reviews management's numbers without an independent expectation.

## Cost-Volume-Profit Analysis in Excel

Cost-volume-profit analysis, commonly known as CVP analysis, is a fundamental technique in managerial accounting that models the relationship between a product's selling price, its variable cost per unit, the total fixed costs associated with producing and selling it, and the resulting profit at various sales volumes. CVP analysis answers questions such as "how many units do we need to sell to break even?" and "how will a ten percent increase in material costs affect our profit?" These are the kinds of questions that the product management team at Charles River wants answered.

The basic CVP model expresses profit as a function of volume:

Profit = (Selling Price per Unit minus Variable Cost per Unit) times Quantity minus Fixed Costs

The term (Selling Price minus Variable Cost) is the contribution margin per unit, the amount each unit contributes toward covering fixed costs and generating profit. When total contribution margin equals total fixed costs, the company breaks even. When total contribution margin exceeds fixed costs, the excess is profit. When total contribution margin falls short of fixed costs, the shortfall is a loss.

Horngren, Datar, and Rajan (2021) describe CVP analysis as one of the most widely used tools in management accounting, noting that its value lies in its ability to clarify the financial consequences of operating decisions before those decisions are made. The simplicity of the model is both its strength and its limitation. CVP analysis assumes that selling price, variable cost per unit, and fixed costs remain constant across the relevant range of volume, and that the company sells everything it produces. These assumptions are approximately true over moderate ranges of volume but break down at extremes. Documenting these assumptions is part of responsible modeling.

### Building a CVP Model

A well-structured CVP model in Excel separates assumptions from calculations. The assumptions section at the top of the worksheet contains the input values that the model depends on: selling price per unit, variable cost per unit, fixed costs, and the range of quantities to evaluate. The calculations section below uses cell references to the assumption cells rather than hard-coded numbers. This structure makes it easy to change an assumption and immediately see the effect on the results, which is the foundation of what-if analysis.

*[Figure 7.8: Layout of a CVP model worksheet. The top section labeled "Assumptions" contains cells for Selling Price ($1,850), Variable Cost per Unit ($1,040), and Fixed Costs ($245,000). The bottom section labeled "Analysis" contains a table with columns for Quantity, Revenue, Total Variable Cost, Total Fixed Cost, Total Cost, Profit, and Contribution Margin Ratio. A cell reference arrow shows that the Revenue formula references the Selling Price cell in the Assumptions section.]*

## What-If Analysis with Scenario Manager and Data Tables

The CVP model you built in Tutorial 7.2 answers questions at a single set of assumptions. But the real value of the model emerges when you ask "what if?" questions. What if material costs increase by ten percent? What if we lower the selling price to gain market share? What if fixed costs increase because we need to add a production shift? Excel provides three tools for systematic what-if analysis: Scenario Manager, data tables, and Goal Seek.

### Scenario Manager

Scenario Manager allows you to define named sets of input values and switch between them to see how the model's outputs change. Each scenario specifies values for one or more input cells. You can create as many scenarios as you need and generate a summary report that compares the results side by side.

To access Scenario Manager, go to the Data tab, click "What-If Analysis," and select "Scenario Manager." In the dialog box, click "Add" to create a new scenario. Give it a name (such as "Base Case"), specify the changing cells (the assumption cells in your model, such as B4, B5, and B6), and enter the values for each cell. Repeat this process for each scenario you want to evaluate.

After creating all scenarios, click "Summary" in the Scenario Manager dialog. Excel asks you to specify the result cells, which are the output cells you want to compare across scenarios (such as the break-even volume and the profit at a specific quantity). Excel then generates a Scenario Summary worksheet that shows each scenario's input values and the corresponding output values in a tabular format.

{{< include _tutorial-03.qmd >}}

### Data Tables for Sensitivity Analysis

While Scenario Manager compares discrete scenarios, a data table shows how an output changes continuously as one or two input values change across a range. A one-variable data table varies a single input and shows the effect on one or more outputs. A two-variable data table varies two inputs simultaneously and shows the effect on a single output.

To create a one-variable data table, set up a column of input values (for example, selling prices ranging from $1,600 to $2,100 in $100 increments) and place formulas that reference the model's output cells in a row adjacent to the top of the input column. Select the range that includes both the input column and the output formulas. Go to the Data tab, click "What-If Analysis," and select "Data Table." In the dialog, specify the Column Input Cell (the assumption cell that the input values should be substituted into). Click OK. Excel fills in the table by calculating each output at every input value in the column.

A two-variable data table works similarly but varies two inputs. The row input values appear across the top, the column input values appear down the left side, and a single output formula is placed in the top-left corner of the table. This is particularly useful for CVP analysis because you can see how profit changes across a range of selling prices and volumes simultaneously.

*[Figure 7.11: A two-variable data table showing profit at varying combinations of Selling Price (columns, from $1,600 to $2,100) and Quantity Sold (rows, from 200 to 600). Cells with negative profit (losses) are formatted in red, and cells with positive profit are formatted in black. The transition from red to black across the table shows how the break-even point shifts as selling price changes.]*

Variable cost is held constant at $1,040 and fixed costs at $245,000. At the current selling price of $1,850, the company breaks even between 300 and 350 units (consistent with the break-even calculation of 303 units). At a lower selling price of $1,600, break-even shifts upward to between 400 and 450 units. At a higher selling price of $2,100, break-even falls to between 250 and 300 units. In the printed version, loss cells are formatted in red and profit cells in black to make the break-even boundary visually apparent.

> **[WATCH OUT]**
> Data tables recalculate automatically every time anything in the workbook changes, which can slow down large workbooks. If your workbook becomes sluggish, you can set the calculation mode to "Automatic Except for Data Tables" in the Formulas tab under Calculation Options. With this setting, data tables update only when you press F9 (recalculate), while all other formulas continue to update automatically.

## Goal Seek and Solver

Scenario Manager and data tables let you explore outcomes across a range of inputs. Goal Seek and Solver work in the opposite direction: they start with a desired outcome and find the input values that produce it.

### Goal Seek

Goal Seek is a simple tool that finds the value of a single input cell that makes a formula cell equal to a specified target. To use it, go to the Data tab, click "What-If Analysis," and select "Goal Seek." The dialog asks for three inputs: the Set Cell (the formula cell whose value you want to control), the To Value (the target value), and the By Changing Cell (the input cell that Goal Seek should adjust).

For example, suppose you want to know what selling price would produce a profit of exactly $200,000 at a volume of 500 units. Set the "Set Cell" to the profit formula at 500 units, set the "To Value" to 200000, and set "By Changing Cell" to the selling price cell. Goal Seek will adjust the selling price until the profit formula equals $200,000. This is a fast way to answer targeted questions without building a full data table.

Goal Seek is limited to adjusting one variable at a time and to finding a single target value. For problems that involve multiple variables, multiple constraints, or an objective to maximize or minimize rather than hit a specific target, you need Solver.

### Solver for Optimization

Solver is an Excel add-in that finds the optimal value of a target cell by adjusting one or more input cells, subject to constraints you define. Unlike Goal Seek, Solver can maximize, minimize, or set a target value, and it can handle problems with multiple decision variables and multiple constraints. These capabilities make Solver the appropriate tool for optimization problems in accounting, such as determining the product mix that maximizes contribution margin, the production schedule that minimizes costs, or the resource allocation that maximizes return.

To enable Solver, follow the same process as for the Data Analysis ToolPak: go to File, Options, Add-ins, select "Solver Add-in," and click Go. Once enabled, Solver appears in the Analysis group on the Data tab.

The Solver dialog asks for several inputs. The Objective is the cell you want to optimize (maximize, minimize, or set to a specific value). The Variable Cells are the cells that Solver can change to achieve the objective. The Constraints are conditions that must be satisfied. Constraints can specify that a cell must be less than or equal to, equal to, or greater than or equal to a value, or that a cell must be an integer.

## Sensitivity Analysis and Documenting Assumptions

Every model depends on assumptions, and the quality of the model's conclusions depends on the quality of those assumptions. Sensitivity analysis is the practice of systematically testing how the model's outputs change when key assumptions change. It answers the question "how wrong can my assumptions be before my conclusions change?" This question is relevant in every accounting context where models are used.

In financial reporting, revenue projections that support going-concern assessments or impairment analyses depend on growth rate assumptions. A sensitivity analysis that shows the projection's conclusion does not change even if the growth rate drops from 5% to 2% provides much stronger support than a projection with no sensitivity testing. In managerial accounting, a CVP model whose break-even conclusion is stable across a wide range of cost assumptions gives management more confidence than one where a small change in variable cost shifts the break-even point dramatically. In auditing, a regression-based expectation that is sensitive to the choice of time period or independent variable should prompt the auditor to consider additional procedures.

The data tables you learned to create in the earlier section are one form of sensitivity analysis. A two-variable data table that shows profit across a range of selling prices and variable costs is a sensitivity analysis of the CVP model. The Solver sensitivity report is another form, showing how the optimal solution changes as constraints are relaxed.

### Documenting Assumptions

Good modeling practice requires that every model include a clear, written documentation of its assumptions. This documentation serves several purposes. It forces the model builder to make assumptions explicit rather than leaving them embedded and invisible. It allows reviewers to evaluate the reasonableness of the assumptions independently. And it provides a basis for updating the model when circumstances change.

An assumption documentation worksheet should include four elements for each key assumption: what the assumption is, what value was used, why that value was chosen (the basis or source), and what the sensitivity of the model's conclusions is to changes in that assumption. Table 7.1 shows an example of this format for the CVP model built in Tutorial 7.2.

*Table 7.1: Example Assumption Documentation for the Beacon Dining Table CVP Model*

| Assumption | Value Used | Basis | Sensitivity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Selling Price per Unit | $1,850 | Item table ListPrice for the Beacon dining table | Break-even increases by approximately 30 units for each $100 decrease in selling price |
| Variable Cost per Unit | $1,040 | Item table StandardCost for the Beacon dining table | Break-even increases by approximately 30 units for each $100 increase in variable cost |
| Fixed Costs (Quarterly) | $245,000 | Estimated allocation of manufacturing overhead, selling, and administrative expenses | Break-even increases by approximately 124 units for each $100,000 increase in fixed costs |
| Relevant Range | 50 to 800 units | Based on historical production levels for this furniture line | Model assumptions may not hold outside this range |

> **[IN PRACTICE]**
> In audit practice, ISA 520 and AU-C Section 520 require that when auditors use analytical procedures as substantive tests, they must document the expectation developed, the data and assumptions used to develop it, the threshold for investigation, and the auditor's conclusion. The assumption documentation approach described here satisfies these requirements and reflects the level of rigor expected in professional analytical work.

Assumption documentation is not a bureaucratic exercise. It is a discipline that improves the quality of analytical work by making the model builder think carefully about what they know, what they are guessing, and where the conclusions are most vulnerable to error. Students who develop this habit early will carry it into professional practice, where the consequences of undocumented assumptions can be significant.

The table includes the four columns described in Table 7.1, with the sensitivity column populated using results from the data table analysis. A callout annotation notes that this documentation would be included as a supporting schedule in a professional report or audit workpaper.]*
